query: The Co-free FeNiCrMn high-entropy alloy is derived from equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi and is intended to retain a favorable strength–ductility balance in its solidified solid-solution state, but its dynamic behavior across different temperatures and strain rates lacks a theoretical explanation. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could account for this behavior, and what controlled comparison within that regime would distinguish it? Specify predictions relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and a falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Dynamic deformation in the Co‐free FeNiCrMn high‐entropy alloy induces a strain-rate and temperature dependent phase transition in the near-surface region from the original coarse-grained structure to an ultra-nanocrystalline/amorphous layer. This transformation produces an inverse Hall–Petch effect that balances strength and ductility under specific loading conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Co‐free FeNiCrMn high‐entropy alloy in a homogeneous, coarse-grained, single‐phase solid-solution state.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled tensile or wear tests at systematically varied strain rates and temperatures in an inert (or ultra-high vacuum) environment.
generation.conditions: The tests should cover a range of strain rates (from low to high) and temperatures (from room temperature to moderately elevated levels) where dynamic deformation can induce microstructural changes without thermal diffusion dominating.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline/amorphous near-surface layer (i.e., dynamic strain-induced grain refinement/amorphization) that mediates the mechanical response.
generation.mechanism: Under specific deformation conditions, the alloy experiences a localized phase transformation at lattice defects and internal boundaries that reduces the effective grain size. This dynamic transformation leads to a regime where the traditional Hall-Petch relationship is inverted, enhancing strength without compromising ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline coarse-grained state (or a Co-containing CoCrFeMnNi alloy), the Co‐free alloy will exhibit increased yield strength and comparable or enhanced ductility under intermediate to high strain rates; this effect should be most pronounced at conditions that favor the dynamic formation of the nanocrystalline/amorphous layer.
generation.baseline: The behavior exhibited by the conventional Co-containing equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy or the same Co-free alloy under low strain-rate (or subcritical temperature) conditions where dynamic phase transition is not activated.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable under inert or ultra-high vacuum conditions and within a specific regime of strain rates and moderate temperatures. It may not apply when thermal effects (e.g., excessive diffusion) or oxidation dominate the microstructural evolution.
generation.uncertainty: The exact thresholds of strain rate and temperature necessary to trigger the transformation are not precisely known, and sample processing variations may influence the onset and extent of the dynamic phase transition.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform a series of tensile or wear experiments on the Co‐free FeNiCrMn alloy at varying strain rates and temperatures, and use high-resolution STEM to monitor the evolution of the grain structure and phase composition (crystalline vs. amorphous) in the near-surface region. For controlled comparison, carry out identical tests on the Co-containing CoCrFeMnNi alloy.
measurements: Yield strength and work hardening rates
Grain size distribution and phase identification (via STEM imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline/amorphous near-surface layer is observed in the Co‐free alloy under conditions where enhanced strength–ductility is expected, or if the mechanical behavior is not significantly different from that of the Co-containing baseline, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
